article_title: Readiness for College
citation: Jenny Nagaoka, Camille A. Farrington, Melissa Roderick, Elaine Allensworth, Tasha Seneca Keyes, David W. Johnson, and Nicole O. Beechum. (2013). Readiness for College: The Role of Noncognitive Factors and Context. VUE (Voices in Urban Education), Fall 2013. https://www.annenberginstitute.org
title: CCSR five-category framework of noncognitive factors
description: The CCSR noncognitive framework organizes research on concepts tied to academic success into five general categories: "academic behaviors, academic perseverance, social skills, learning strategies, and academic mindsets." It was designed to synthesize a vast research literature, clarify meanings, and reconcile disparities between researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds. In the framework, mindsets and learning strategies feed academic behaviors and perseverance, which together produce academic performance, all nested within school, socio-cultural, community, and policy contexts.
requirements: Practitioners keep the mechanisms that affect persistence (mindsets, skills, strategies) conceptually distinct so interventions can be designed effectively
constraints: The framework keeps related concepts such as grit, tenacity, self-control, and delayed gratification distinct from the degree to which one persists in academic work
target_learning_goals: academic performance
persistence and college attainment
examples: Figure 1 depicts the framework, mapping individual-level factors through school and classroom context to college readiness dimensions of academic preparedness, college knowledge, and academic tenacity
key_sources: Jenny Nagaoka, Camille A. Farrington, Melissa Roderick, Elaine Allensworth, Tasha Seneca Keyes, David W. Johnson, and Nicole O. Beechum. (2013). Readiness for College: The Role of Noncognitive Factors and Context. VUE (Voices in Urban Education), Fall 2013. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/readiness-college-role-noncognitive-factors-and-context

article_title: The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, an Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3
citation: Jonathan Nakamoto, Sandy Sobolew-Shubin, Martin Orland. (2015). The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, An Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Comprehensive Cross Unit (CCU) Assessments measuring Cross-Unit DEEP literacy and life skills
description: The CCU Assessments (Joy, Ruth, and Jackie Tests) were developed specifically for the A4L curriculum by Dr. Diana Sharp with University of Washington experts, and assess Cross-Unit skills rather than Unit-Specific skills. Cross-Unit items assess "DEEP skills (Decision Enhanced by Empathy and Perspective)", including describing a character's or author's traits, emotions, thoughts, or internal motivations and analyzing how perspective impacts genre-specific elements. The tests use open-ended questions scored with rubrics of nine (Joy) or 12 (Ruth, Jackie) criteria, with printed Cronbach's alphas of .70-.75 (Joy), .77-.82 (Ruth), and .80/.79 (Jackie pre/post).
requirements: administered as fall pre-test and spring post-test after the Residency
scoring overseen by a trained literacy expert using shared rubrics
constraints: validity studies have not been conducted on the CCU Assessments and no parallel forms exist; convergent validity correlations with the OAKS ranged from r = .62 to r = .68
target_learning_goals: literacy achievement
21st century learning and life skills such as empathy and perspective-taking
examples: The Joy Test was administered to grade 3 and the Ruth Test to grade 4 in all three study years
key_sources: Jonathan Nakamoto, Sandy Sobolew-Shubin, Martin Orland. (2015). The Beaverton School District Arts for Learning (A4L) Lessons Project, An Investing in Innovation (i3) Development Grant: Student Impact Findings from Years 1, 2, and 3. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED560945

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: cc-self-train adaptive learning system: a three-layer hook-based engagement observation and scaffolding adjustment mechanism
description: The adaptive learning system observes learner engagement quality through keyword-heuristic classification of each learner message into six engagement categories with quality scores from 1 to 5, accumulated in a local learner profile. Layer 1 is a silent Stop hook that fires after every Claude response and computes streak booleans; Layer 2 injects a teaching note into Claude's context at session start based on the productive/unproductive ratio; Layer 3 adjusts the learner's Effective Level at module boundaries. The article describes "a two-timescale system" in which a slow clock adjusts the persona schedule at module boundaries using aggregate statistics while a fast clock triggers scaffolding changes mid-module using sequential patterns, governed by an asymmetric response principle that is quicker to increase scaffolding than to withdraw it.
requirements: Operates entirely through Claude Code's hook system with no external dependencies, no API calls for observation, and no web backend
constraints: Observation uses keyword heuristics rather than LLM-based classification, so individual classifications are noisy; Effective Level changes occur only at module boundaries; level changes are silent to the student
target_learners: developers learning an agentic AI coding tool through the cc-self-train curriculum
target_learning_goals: sustained productive engagement and appropriately paced scaffolding during tool-mastery learning
examples: A struggle streak (three or more consecutive answer_seeking or passive_acceptance classifications) produces the priority alert "Offer more scaffolding NOW"
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: Agentic Education with AI Coding Assistants
citation: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460
title: cc-self-train auto-updating sync pipeline: an onboarding agent that detects upstream tool changes and updates teaching materials before instruction begins
description: The sync pipeline (/sync skill) addresses the content decay problem of curricula for rapidly evolving tools. The article states: "when a learner begins the curriculum, the onboarding agent checks whether its teaching materials cover the learner's installed version of Claude Code. If not, it updates the modules before instruction begins, so the learner always receives a current snapshot." The six-step pipeline detects the version gap, fetches and triages the upstream changelog, maps features to affected modules, researches new features, updates module and context files, and verifies structural integrity, reverting any file that fails. A safe-append rule never modifies or renumbers existing steps, inserting new content before the Checkpoint section.
requirements: A predefined feature-to-module mapping and a parametrized test suite that verifies structural integrity of updated files
constraints: During onboarding only the learner's chosen project variant is updated; standalone maintainer invocation updates all five variants in bulk
target_learners: developers learning agentic AI coding tools whose features change on a cadence measured in days
target_learning_goals: learning current tool features rather than outdated curriculum content
examples: Adding BYOP as a 5th path required generating 10 module files, which the pipeline then maintains alongside the original 40
key_sources: Zain Naboulsi. (2026). Agentic Education: Using Claude Code to Teach Claude Code. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17460

article_title: Using AI-Generated Feedback to Improve Critical Thinking and Writing Proficiency
citation: Qi Zhu, Xiaoming Zhai, Yan Zou, Chunlei Gao. (2026). Using AI-Generated Feedback to Improve Critical Thinking and Writing Proficiency. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4519-1931
title: CCTDI-to-writing-rubric mapping framework linking critical thinking dispositions to writing performance indicators
description: The study establishes a conceptual mapping between the California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory (CCTDI) framework and a customized writing rubric, so that cognitive dispositions are measured through writing performance. As the article states, "the core CCTDI dimensions were operationalized into specific writing performance indicators" (e.g., Open-mindedness to Perspective Diversification & Bias Identification; Truth-seeking to Evidence Sourcing & Argumentation Depth). The framework was developed from the Compulsory Education Curriculum Standards for Chinese (2022 Edition) and refined through expert synthesis and teacher deliberation, underpinning both WISE Agent feedback generation and outcome measurement.
requirements: Developed through a theoretical review by five pedagogy specialists followed by collaborative deliberations among 14 senior language teachers.
constraints: Adapted to suit elementary cognitive characteristics; the disposition scale serves as a measure of potential activated through iterative writing tasks.
target_learners: Elementary students in a cognitive transition phase (grade 6)
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking dispositions expressed through writing quality and argumentation
examples: The two-dimensional evaluation framework encompassed writing quality (organization, objectivity, and argumentation depth) and critical thinking (logical reasoning, multiple perspectives, and dialectical analysis).
key_sources: Qi Zhu, Xiaoming Zhai, Yan Zou, Chunlei Gao. (2026). Using AI-Generated Feedback to Improve Critical Thinking and Writing Proficiency. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4519-1931

article_title: Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition
citation: Paritosh Parmar, Landy Lan, Hong Yang, Chen Yi, Chiat Pin Tay. (2026). Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05115
title: CCTV-view classroom incident recognition benchmark (synthetic plus real-world preschool pose data)
description: A hybrid benchmark for privacy-aware classroom incident recognition combining AI-generated CCTV-style synthetic videos with real-world preschool recordings represented as anonymized pose data. It covers seven action classes {fall, punch, jump, kick, throw, run, sit} plus a background meta-class of ordinary classroom actions, and comprises 1296 synthetic samples and 574 real-world samples annotated with poses, action classes, and temporal boundaries. The authors state "we will release the resulting dataset to support research in classroom incident recognition."
requirements: Annotation via the authors' integrated annotation toolbox, which preloads time-consuming annotations such as skeletal poses for correction rather than from-scratch labeling
Quality validation by preschool teachers acting as domain experts, with rejected samples discarded
constraints: The released dataset will contain only synthetic videos and approved real-world predicted skeleton keypoints, with no personally identifiable or linkable student or teacher information
The background class increases the difficulty of the classification task
target_learners: preschool students and teachers in monitored classrooms
target_learning_goals: recognition of safety-relevant classroom incidents such as falls, fights, running, throwing, and distress-related behaviors
examples: Videos were generated with Kling and Seedance after a preliminary study of several generators, reviewed independently by three authors, and validated by preschool teachers
key_sources: Paritosh Parmar, Landy Lan, Hong Yang, Chen Yi, Chiat Pin Tay. (2026). Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05115

article_title: Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers
citation: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756
title: Design CCT for older adults as supervised group-based training at 1–3 sessions per week with sessions of at least 30 minutes
description: The review's moderator analyses ground a design principle: efficacy in healthy older adults "is to a large extent determined by design choices." Group-based delivery (g = 0.29) and 1–3 weekly sessions were effective, while home-based delivery and more than three sessions per week were ineffective, and sessions shorter than 30 min showed only weak evidence of efficacy. The authors conclude that "Consistently ineffective design choices should therefore be avoided."
requirements: Group-based delivery with a trainer present to support adherence, fidelity, and motivation, as the article describes group-based practice variables
constraints: Evidence limited to healthy older adults without dementia or MCI; durability of gains not addressed
Sessions shorter than 30 min show only weak evidence of efficacy
target_learning_goals: improving cognitive performance, particularly processing speed, nonverbal memory, working memory, and visuospatial skills
examples: Future studies incorporating supervised group-based delivery and a session frequency of 2–3 sessions per week can anticipate an approximate effect size of g = 0.29, per the authors' power calculation
key_sources: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756

article_title: Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers
citation: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756
title: CCT program content taxonomy: speed of processing, working memory, attention, multidomain, and video games
description: The review classifies CCT interventions into five content types: "speed of processing (SOP) training, WM training, attention training, multidomain training, and video games." Video games are defined as computer programs distributed for entertainment purposes before being tried as cognitive interventions. Across the 52 included datasets, 24 studies used multidomain training, nine SOP, nine WM, six attention, and four video games, with delivery split between group-based (61.5%) and home-based (36.5%) settings.
requirements: Programs must involve at least 4 h of practice on standardized computerized tasks or video games with clear cognitive rationale
constraints: Lab-specific interventions not involving computer interaction were excluded from the review's scope
target_learning_goals: enhancing cognitive performance across multiple domains
examples: Included programs ranged from commercial packages (CogniFit, Lumosity, Brain Fitness) to in-house programs and entertainment video games such as Rise of Nations and Tetris
key_sources: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756

article_title: Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children
citation: Davis, S., Rawlings, B., Clegg, J. M., Ikejimba, D., Watson-Jones, R. E., Whiten, A. & Legare, C. H. (2022). Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18231-7
title: Cumulative cultural evolution requires behavioral switching and maintenance of adopted improvements
description: The article frames cumulative cultural evolution (CCE) as "the process of accumulating knowledge and skills that increases the complexity and/or efficiency of technology and other forms of culture over time". It decomposes CCE into switching (relinquishing a current behavior for an improved version) and maintenance (resisting reversion to earlier versions and omitting redundant actions), arguing cognitive flexibility underpins these processes and their ontogeny in childhood.
requirements: Successful CCE requires both behavioral switching to improved versions and maintenance of what has been adopted
constraints: The framework is developed and tested with U.S. children aged 3–5 in a puzzlebox task
target_learning_goals: flexibly switching to more efficient solutions
maintaining adopted solutions and omitting redundant actions
examples: Children learned an inefficient Serialbox method by demonstration, witnessed a more efficient method, and were given multiple further interaction opportunities
key_sources: Davis, S., Rawlings, B., Clegg, J. M., Ikejimba, D., Watson-Jones, R. E., Whiten, A. & Legare, C. H. (2022). Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18231-7

article_title: Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures
citation: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797
title: Case's central conceptual structures theory, reconsidered with working memory capacity as the developmental driver of quantitative concepts
description: The article reconsiders Case's theory of central conceptual structures (CCS), which describes qualitative developmental levels in children's quantitative concepts. Its lead hypothesis is that "the development of working memory capacity shapes the development of quantitative concepts (whole and rational numbers)". The two studies operationalize whole-number and rational-number CCS as measurable structures whose acquisition is tied to working memory units. Overall, the authors state that "the results support Case's CCS theory and clarify the role of working memory in the acquisition of numerical concepts."
requirements: Measures of the whole-number and rational-number CCS validated against children's working memory capacity
constraints: Evidence reported here covers children from preschool to grade 5 (whole number) and sixth- and seventh-graders (rational number)
target_learning_goals: whole number understanding
rational number understanding
key_sources: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797

article_title: Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science
citation: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9
title: Bridges model: professional, citizen, and student bridges connecting schools with communities outside school, linked by a learning circle
description: The article proposes a preliminary conceptual model of how community and citizen science projects connect schools with communities outside school. It defines three bridges: "The citizen bridge connects citizen communities and schools; the professional bridge connects professional communities and schools; and the student bridge connects new types of student communities and schools." A learning circle links the bridges through citizenship learning, community learning, and profession learning, with the educational design focus shifting by proximity to each bridge. The model frames the design and analysis of the two urban development projects.
requirements: CCS projects must attend to all three bridges to support the rich, cross-cutting goals they are purported to achieve
constraints: The model is preliminary and "requires further empirical work to both explicate and validate it"
target_learners: K–12 students, specifically students aged 11–15 in vulnerable residential areas
target_learning_goals: Connecting school learning to professional, citizen, and student community practices, values, and knowledge
examples: The two DBR iterations, Cities at Play and Community Drive, were designed and analyzed through the bridges model, with the second iteration strengthening the professional bridge
key_sources: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9

article_title: Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law
citation: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3
title: Conceptual Change Model applied to civic and political concepts
description: The article adopts the Conceptual Change Model (Posner et al., 1982) as its theoretical framework for civic education, arguing that political misconceptions are rooted in intuitive folk theories and media interpretations and resist mere informational correction. Learning occurs through interaction between new and pre-existing concepts, with change occurring through shifts in concept status. The article states: "The four essential conditions for Conceptual Change underlying the CCM are: dissatisfaction with the existing concept, intelligibility of the new concept, plausibility of the new concept, and fruitfulness of the new concept." The study's activities were designed to create cognitive conflict (dissatisfaction) and establish the new civic concepts as intelligible, plausible, and fruitful.
requirements: Instruction must deliberately create cognitive conflict highlighting shortcomings of learners' current comprehension, since deeply rooted misconceptions cannot be corrected simply by adding new information
constraints: The article notes civic-domain misconceptions are rooted in folk theories and disputed knowledge, making identification and evaluation of mistakes harder than in science domains
target_learning_goals: Understanding of republic, democracy, and the state of law
Conceptual change in civic and political concepts
examples: The study's concept cartoons were used to elicit initial alternative concepts and encourage cognitive conflict, followed by journaling, concept mapping, and poster activities addressing the remaining CCM conditions
key_sources: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3

article_title: Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies
citation: Aleknavičiūtė, V., Lehtinen, E., & Södervik, I. (2023). Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100556
title: Conceptual change theory landscape: Posner's conditions model most used in biology interventions, alongside Vosniadou's framework theory and Chi's ontological shift
description: The review organises intervention studies by the conceptual change theory each builds on, coding papers into 14 framework groups (Posner, Chi, Vosniadou, diSessa, Carey, Driver, Nussbaum and Novick, Clement, Klein, Duit, Pintrich, Sinatra, multidimensional CC theory, and no CC theory). Posner's theory, which holds that learners must be "dissatisfied with existing conceptions and view scientific concepts as meaningful, plausible and fruitful", was the most frequently cited basis for biology interventions. Vosniadou's and Chi's theories were used equally frequently, with Chi's ontological shift theory particularly common in evolution interventions and usually combined with other theories. Nineteen studies referenced no conceptual change theory at all.
requirements: Interventions applying these theories should make learners aware of the conflict between prior thinking and new concepts, as the theory theories prescribe
constraints: Chi's ontological shift theory was more often combined with other CC theories than used as the sole basis for interventions
19 intervention studies did not refer to any specific theory of conceptual change
target_learners: kindergarten through university students, including natural science majors and student teachers
target_learning_goals: restructuring of biological misconceptions toward scientifically accepted understanding
examples: The review coded all 96 articles by theoretical framework and found Posner's theory applied across topics from climate change to genetics and respiration, with populations from lower secondary to college students.
key_sources: Aleknavičiūtė, V., Lehtinen, E., & Södervik, I. (2023). Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100556

article_title: Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework
citation: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x
title: Four-domain taxonomy of classroom resource and limiting factors: external, collective classroom, teacher, and individual student
description: The CCC framework organizes resource and limiting factors across four interdependent domains "external, collective classroom, teacher, and individual student," built from previous conceptual models. External factors include teacher-caregiver partnerships, school climate, and neighborhood conditions; collective classroom factors include aggregate student group characteristics and supplies; teacher factors include self-efficacy, burnout, and health; student factors include relationship perceptions, social-emotional skills, sleep quality, and food insecurity. The domains are conceptualized as interdependent with interactive and potentially additive influence on Classroom Carrying Capacity.
requirements: The delineation is intended to assist stakeholders and researchers in conceptualizing and organizing research questions, teacher training, approaches to measurement, and theories of change
constraints: The authors note "these domains do not include an exhaustive list of factors"; the goal is to guide future identification and study of resource and limiting factors
target_learning_goals: Understanding how multi-level classroom factors cumulatively influence student functioning and development
examples: Table 1 presents a conceptualization of environmental, psychosocial, density-dependent, and density-independent factors across the four domains
key_sources: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x

article_title: Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework
citation: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x
title: Categorization schema for classroom factors: density dependent vs. independent and psychosocial vs. environmental
description: The framework operationalizes classroom factors along two dimensions: density dependency and type. The framework "operationalizes these factors by introducing dimensions of density dependency (dependent vs. independent) and type (psychosocial vs. environmental), enabling a systematic evaluation of their cumulative and interactive effects on classroom outcomes." Density-dependent factors (e.g., instructional time, student-teacher ratios) change in effect as collective student needs increase, while density-independent factors (e.g., classroom space, teacher training) affect support quality regardless of density. Environmental factors are tangible (space, materials, time), psychosocial factors include efficacy, relationships, and behaviors.
requirements: Researchers should define measurements of CCC, in part, by their density (dependent vs. independent) and whether they are physical or psychosocial across the four domains
constraints: The authors state these categorizations attribute importance to varying and multiple, potentially cumulative factors, and that malleability and influence of factors may differ in strength
target_learning_goals: Systematic evaluation of cumulative and interactive effects of classroom factors on student outcomes
examples: A fixed amount of instructional time for a reading lesson is density dependent: when collective student needs are high, available time becomes insufficient, leaving some students without their required intensity of instruction
key_sources: Kristen L. Granger, Jason C. Chow. (2025). Classroom Carrying Capacity: A Resource and Limiting Factors Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09999-x

article_title: Applying collaborative cognitive load theory to computer-supported collaborative learning: towards a research agenda
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Paul A. Kirschner. (2020). Applying collaborative cognitive load theory to computer-supported collaborative learning: towards a research agenda. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09729-5
title: Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory (CCLT)
description: CCLT extends cognitive load theory to (computer-supported) collaborative learning by treating groups of collaborative learners as information processing systems. Its core concepts are collective working memory (individuals "share the burden of information processing"), mutual cognitive interdependence (group members learn about and depend on each other's expertise), and transaction costs (the working-memory burden of communication and coordination). The article uses CCLT to formulate testable hypotheses and design guidelines for CSCL.
requirements: Effectiveness depends on the balance between the distribution advantage and the transaction costs incurred by transactive activities
constraints: Whether CSCL is effective depends on the balance struck between distribution advantage and transaction costs; when transaction costs exceed the distribution advantage, individual learning is more effective
target_learners: students in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge acquisition through collaboration
examples: The article applies CCLT to hypothesize about student, group, task, and technological characteristics affecting CSCL
key_sources: Jeroen Janssen, Paul A. Kirschner. (2020). Applying collaborative cognitive load theory to computer-supported collaborative learning: towards a research agenda. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09729-5

article_title: Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning
citation: Susana Sánchez Castro, Mª Ángeles Pascual Sevillano, Rogelio Buceta Otero, Javier Fombona Cadavieco. (2026). Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10744-6
title: Creative Computational Problem Solving (CCPS) model: five interactive phases structuring computational thinking development through creative problem solving with programming and robotics
description: The CCPS model (Chevalier et al., 2020, 2021) is a framework for structuring the development of computational thinking in educational settings, described by the article as "one of the most comprehensive and validated frameworks" in this area. It organizes learning through creative problem solving and integrates programming and educational robotics as central tools. It is structured around five interactive phases: Understanding, Idea Generation, Formalization, Implementation/Programming, and Evaluation, in which outcomes are analyzed, errors debugged, and processes improved iteratively. This study operationalized the five phases through a two-hour workshop with rotating stations and guided creative challenges.
requirements: Operational frameworks are needed to guide educational practice in specific contexts; the phases must be operationalized through concrete activities such as rotating stations and guided creative challenges
constraints: The article notes TPACK lacks a specific operational guide for structuring the teaching of CT or machine learning and needs complementing by more concrete, situated models; CCPS is applied here only as a two-hour initial-exposure microintervention, not sustained competency development
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
creative problem solving
programming and robotics familiarity
examples: The workshop operationalized the five phases: students understood proposed challenges, generated ideas, formalized solutions using mental diagrams or programming blocks, implemented tasks in Scratch, micro:bit, or Makey Makey, and reviewed outcomes to refine proposals
key_sources: Susana Sánchez Castro, Mª Ángeles Pascual Sevillano, Rogelio Buceta Otero, Javier Fombona Cadavieco. (2026). Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10744-6

article_title: Classroom Connectivity and Algebra 1 Achievement: A Three-Year Longitudinal Study
citation: Irving, K. E., Pape, S. J., Owens, D. T., Abrahamson, L., Silver, D., & Sanalan, V. A. (2016). Classroom Connectivity and Algebra 1 Achievement: A Three-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Computers in Mathematics and Science Teaching, 35(2), 131-151. https://www.jcmst.org
title: CCT active-learning framework: broadened representational infrastructure and timely feedback loops improving formative assessment
description: The article's theoretical framework holds that connected classroom technology supports active learning environments that "broaden the representational infrastructure of the classroom" and provide "timely, targeted, and accurate feedback loops" that improve formative assessment opportunities and ultimately algebra 1 achievement. CCT serves as a mediating tool between mathematical content and classroom culture, transferring responsibility for mathematical thinking to students through public display of tasks, anonymous participation, and simultaneous display of multiple mathematical representations. The framework was used to design the professional development intervention and to interpret the trial's achievement gains.
requirements: Teachers must participate in professional development (a summer institute and follow-up) alongside the technology; the article argues the intervention includes both CCT and teacher professional development
constraints: Simply providing equipment to teachers has not been demonstrated to make a difference in teaching or learning, per the article
target_learners: algebra 1 students in secondary mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: algebra 1 achievement
mathematical communication and discourse
representational fluency
examples: The trial's treatment teachers attended a one-week residential summer institute and yearly technology-conference follow-up before implementing the TI Navigator system with Quick Poll, Learning Check, Screen Capture, and Activity Center components

article_title: The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the Symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates
citation: Batdal Karaduman, G. (2019). The Effects of Conceptual Change Texts Enriched with Metaconceptual Activities on the symmetry of Classroom Teacher Candidates. Acta Didactica Napocensia, 12(1), 107-116. https://doi.org/10.24193/adn.12.1.7
title: Conceptual change texts enriched with metaconceptual activities
description: Conceptual change texts are used "in the process of conceptual change and displacement of the misconceptions of students with the scientific ones" (attributed to Köse, 2011); the enriched version is gathered "by adding metaconceptual activities in conceptual change texts" (attributed to Demir, 2010). The article's symmetry texts open by probing learners' existing ideas, present example dilemmas with fictional students' answers to choose among, then give the scientific explanation and prompt re-evaluation, re-summarization, and redrawing of concept maps.
requirements: Knowledge of the common misconceptions in the target topic, obtained from the literature, so the text can target them
constraints: Evaluated here only with undergraduate teacher candidates on the topic of symmetry
target_learning_goals: Replacing symmetry misconceptions with scientific concepts
examples: Example 1 asks with whom the candidate agrees about a square's symmetry axes, contrasting the ideas that there is always a single axis and that there are four axes

article_title: Investigating the Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Shima Rajabi, Akbar Azizifar, & Habib Gowhary. (2015). Investigating the of Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.53
title: CCSARP taxonomy of seven apology strategies
description: The article adopts the cross-cultural speech act realization project (CCSARP) taxonomy as its framework for apology strategies. It states that "a very common taxonomy was the basis of the cross-cultural speech act realization project (CCSARP), and it consists of seven strategies to perform apologies", including illocutionary force indicating devices, taking on responsibility, explanation, offer of repair, and promise of forbearance. The strategies "can be used, according to authors, by themselves or in any combination or sequence". The study taught apology strategies grounded in this taxonomy and scored responses using Afghary's (2007) RESP categorization.
requirements: Taxonomies of apology strategies should be applied with respect to the respective culture, since the speech act is culture specific
constraints: The article notes diversity in apology classifications resulting from cross-cultural differences
target_learners: Iranian EFL learners at intermediate and advanced levels
target_learning_goals: Appropriate production of apology speech act strategies in the target language
examples: The treatment groups received instruction in apology strategies for half an hour, ten minutes per speech act, alongside regular institute instruction
key_sources: Shima Rajabi, Akbar Azizifar, & Habib Gowhary. (2015). Investigating the of Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.53

article_title: Online Argumentation Implementation in the Development of Critical Thinking Disposition
citation: Fettahlıoğlu, P., & Kaleci, D. (2018). Online Argumentation Implementation in the Development of Critical Thinking Disposition. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i3.2904
title: California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory (CCTDI) as outcome measure
description: The study used the California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory, a six-point Likert measure with a score range of 51-306, adapted to Turkish by Kökdemir (2003) with 51 items and six subscales. The whole-scale internal consistency was .88 in the adaptation and a pilot with 152 education students found a Cronbach Alpha of .79 before use in this study.
requirements: Pilot reliability check before use (Cronbach Alpha .79 in this study's pilot)
constraints: Subscales were not used in this study; only total scores
target_learning_goals: measuring disposition to think critically
examples: Applied as pre-test in week 1 and post-test at the end of week 12
key_sources: Fettahlıoğlu, P., & Kaleci, D. (2018). Online Argumentation Implementation in the Development of Critical Thinking Disposition. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i3.2904

article_title: Nursing Students' Perceptions of a Clinical Simulation Experience in Community Care: Strengths and Limitations.
citation: Gómez‐Torres, P., S. Galarreta‐Aperte, I. Blázquez‐Ornat, I. Antón‐Solanas, and E. Ramón‐Arbués. (2026). Nursing Students' Perceptions of a Clinical Simulation Experience in Community Care: Strengths and Limitations. Nursing Open 13, no. 9: e70807. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70807
title: Four faculty-designed community care simulation scenarios in a high-fidelity laboratory with prebriefing, enactment and debriefing
description: A clinical simulation activity for a 6-ECTS second-year Health Education course. "Four faculty members designed the activity collaboratively. They selected four topics, namely diabetes, hypertension, vaccination schedules and contraceptive counselling, and developed the corresponding scenarios for implementation in the university's high‐fidelity simulation laboratory and debriefing room." Each session lasted approximately 45 minutes and comprised prebriefing, scenario enactment and debriefing; one student per scenario acted as the primary care nurse while peers observed, with all students joining debriefing.
requirements: Faculty with active clinical practice to develop authentic and clinically relevant scenarios
constraints: Only one student participated directly in each scenario while the others observed, creating unequal opportunities for hands-on involvement
target_learning_goals: Applying the nursing process and initiating health education tasks with primary health care patients
examples: Scenarios included a 52-year-old hypertensive male, a 6-month well-child visit with a high-fidelity paediatric mannequin, a newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetes patient, and contraceptive counselling in a midwife consultation.
key_sources: Gómez‐Torres, P., S. Galarreta‐Aperte, I. Blázquez‐Ornat, I. Antón‐Solanas, and E. Ramón‐Arbués. (2026). Nursing Students' Perceptions of a Clinical Simulation Experience in Community Care: Strengths and Limitations. Nursing Open 13, no. 9: e70807. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70807

article_title: Tactical and assessment competency gaps in pre-service coaches: evidence from a game-based implementation.
citation: Acar Eyup & Akinci Yasin. (2026). Tactical and assessment competency gaps in pre-service coaches: evidence from a game-based implementation. Scientific Reports 16, 23736. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-53681-3
title: Coaching Content Knowledge and Occupational Socialization Theory as the framework for educator game-playing competency
description: The article frames game-based instructional competency through Coaching Content Knowledge (CCK), which "integrates elements such as the coach's subject matter knowledge (rules, techniques), pedagogical knowledge (instructional strategies), and context knowledge (athletes' developmental stages)", operationalised as Tactical Competency. It combines CCK with Occupational Socialization Theory, particularly Lortie's "apprenticeship of observation", to hypothesize differential competency development between CE and PET pathways. Tactical Competency is defined as the coach's skill in reading game flow and making timely interventions.
requirements: Game-based success depends on the educator's ability to design, manage, stop, ask critical questions, and evaluate the game
constraints: The study examines how pre-service coaches and teachers are prepared to apply LTAD/DSPM models, rather than the models themselves
target_learning_goals: tactical competency in game-based instruction
assessment and reflective evaluation competency
examples: The study used CCK and OST to formulate hypotheses H1-H3 about differential CE/PET competency development
key_sources: Acar Eyup & Akinci Yasin. (2026). Tactical and assessment competency gaps in pre-service coaches: evidence from a game-based implementation. Scientific Reports 16, 23736. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-53681-3

article_title: When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education.
citation: Al-Shawee N, McElvaney G, Strawbridge J, Spooner M. (2026). When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2033
title: Co-Created SBA Design (CCSD) framework: a triadic model of educator, institution, and GenAI collaboration for AI-assisted item-writing
description: The CCSD framework reconceptualises SBA assessment design for the GenAI era by positioning educators, institutions, and GenAI as interdependent collaborators operating within Van der Vleuten's Utility Index. As the article states, "Within this triadic model, each contributor plays a distinct yet complementary role in sustaining assessment quality." The framework delineates responsibilities (what must be done) while the Utility Index dimensions clarify why they matter, mapping how "institutional governance, educator expertise, and GenAI capability interact, both directly and indirectly." It is presented as a roadmap for responsible GenAI integration rather than an empirically tested model.
requirements: Educator expertise and institutional guidance and training are considered essential, co-existing concepts to GenAI for its application in assessment
constraints: The framework is a conceptual Eye Opener; its value depends on how effectively the three pillars manage trade-offs across Utility Index dimensions
target_learners: Medical and health professions educators writing SBA/MCQ assessment items
target_learning_goals: Designing valid, reliable, educationally impactful SBA items with GenAI assistance
examples: Figure 1 places assessment items at the centre, surrounded by the educator (academic expertise and oversight), institutions (governance, infrastructure, training), and GenAI (adaptability, scalability, efficiency)
key_sources: Al-Shawee N, McElvaney G, Strawbridge J, Spooner M. (2026). When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2033

article_title: Cartooning in Biological Learning.
citation: Bahsoun Soukaina, Morris Mhairi, Akam Elizabeth. (2026). Cartooning in Biological Learning. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.70040
title: Concept Cartooning Student-Centered Learning (CCSCL): a five-aspect framework for student-centered cartooning seminars
description: The article proposes CCSCL, applying the five aspects of student-centered learning in higher education to cartooning seminars. The teacher's role is a "Cartoon and content guide, act as the facilitator of learning"; content serves skill acquisition rather than memorizing biological cascades as lists; responsibility for learning is shared; evaluation is a means to learn, practice skills and give and receive feedback; and the balance of power is dynamic and changeable based on the facilitator's pedagogical leanings. The framework is grounded in the study's seminar design and survey evidence.
requirements: Students and teachers must work in partnership, with students putting forth effort and institutions providing an appropriate environment to facilitate learning
constraints: The balance of power was not fully evaluated within this study and requires further consideration; if not managed carefully it may create confusion, uneven participation, or gaps in guidance
target_learning_goals: understanding complex multi-step biological processes
higher-order thinking beyond remembering
collaboration and communication skills
examples: Seminars in three biology modules where students formed teams of two to six, drew cartoons of randomly chosen subtopics, presented them, and peer-ranked other groups' cartoons with aggregated points
key_sources: Bahsoun Soukaina, Morris Mhairi, Akam Elizabeth. (2026). Cartooning in Biological Learning. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.70040

article_title: Computer-based case simulations enhances clinical reasoning skills of non-dental medical students as measured by mini-CEX.
citation: Zeng Jiahao, Geng Yuanming, Zhang Jingwen, Liu Chundong, Liu Xin, Shen Xiaoqing, Lv Xiaozhi, Zhou Xiaolong. (2026). Computer-based case simulations enhances clinical reasoning skills of non-dental medical students as measured by mini-CEX. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08593-1
title: Computer-based Case Simulations (CCS) program for stomatology clerkship training
description: A computer-based case simulation program built with Blender for three-dimensional modeling and Unity for logical coding, using the 9th-edition Stomatology textbook as reference. It integrates "oral examination techniques, patient history acquisition, etiological analysis, diagnostic methodologies, disease identification, and treatment planning", with diagnosis and treatment planning presented as multiple choice questions and interactive videos of common oral cases hosted on Bilibili. It was implemented in the intervention group's clerkship to emulate clinical reasoning processes.
requirements: Developed jointly by the Department of Stomatology, Zhujiang Hospital, Southern Medical University and the Department of Orthodontics, Guangzhou Medical University School and Hospital of Stomatology
constraints: Prioritized diagnostic workflows over procedural training, aligned to non-dental students' needs
target_learners: fourth-year non-dentistry medical undergraduates in stomatology clerkship
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning in stomatology
oral disease diagnosis and treatment planning
examples: Used during the stomatology clerkship with standardized oral examination techniques and interactive case videos on the Bilibili website
key_sources: Zeng Jiahao, Geng Yuanming, Zhang Jingwen, Liu Chundong, Liu Xin, Shen Xiaoqing, Lv Xiaozhi, Zhou Xiaolong. (2026). Computer-based case simulations enhances clinical reasoning skills of non-dental medical students as measured by mini-CEX. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08593-1

article_title: Computer-based case simulations enhances clinical reasoning skills of non-dental medical students as measured by mini-CEX.
citation: Zeng Jiahao, Geng Yuanming, Zhang Jingwen, Liu Chundong, Liu Xin, Shen Xiaoqing, Lv Xiaozhi, Zhou Xiaolong. (2026). Computer-based case simulations enhances clinical reasoning skills of non-dental medical students as measured by mini-CEX. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08593-1
title: CCS–Mini-CEX integration as an operationalization of Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle
description: The authors frame their intervention as aligning with Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, in which "individuals repeatedly go through four stages during learning: experience, reflection, theorization and action". In their account, concrete virtual patient experiences via CCS are followed by reflective observation and abstract conceptualization through Mini-CEX feedback, rather than simply embedding content in the computer system. Using the Mini-CEX as the outcome measure lets students experience real clinical environments and receive timely teaching feedback.
requirements: Pairing simulation-based concrete experience with a timely feedback mechanism
constraints: Framed by the authors for stomatology education of non-dental medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning skills
translating theoretical knowledge into clinical practice
examples: CCS virtual patient encounters followed by Mini-CEX feedback sessions in the clerkship

article_title: Effects of virtual reality-based disaster simulation education on nursing students.
citation: Kim Kyeng-Jin, Choi Moon-Ji, Kim MinJi. (2025). Effects of virtual reality-based disaster simulation education on nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329563
title: VR disaster triage simulation program based on cognitive continuum theory with START/Jump START triage
description: A ~30-minute VR disaster simulation for Oculus Quest 2 in which learners triage six casualty cases using the START and Jump START protocols, checking breathing rate, pulse, and consciousness in a realistic mass-casualty scene. Its design embeds four CCT learning elements—analytical cognition, situational awareness, cognitive control, and self-awareness—followed by structured debriefing. The program "was deemed appropriate, with a content validity index (CVI) of.80 or above, as assessed by two nursing professors, one disaster educator, and one nurse."
requirements: Requires VR equipment (Oculus Quest 2), a practice room, pre-learning on disaster triage, and instructors with VR and disaster nursing qualifications
constraints: Training split into two ~15-minute sessions to reduce VR side effects; a guardian system turns off the virtual screen if users leave the set space
target_learners: Third- and fourth-year undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: Disaster triage accuracy and speed
Disaster triage confidence
Cognitive flexibility
Learning immersion
examples: In a VR situation, the patient's breathing rate and pulse were measured directly, and their level of consciousness was confirmed by asking their name or about the weather
key_sources: Kim Kyeng-Jin, Choi Moon-Ji, Kim MinJi. (2025). Effects of virtual reality-based disaster simulation education on nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329563

article_title: Psychometric Evaluation of the Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Scale for Disaster Rescue Nurses in Mainland China.
citation: Lai Jinjia, Chen Hongyi, Huang Yongqi, Ma Chaoqun, Zeng Ping, Chen Hanxi, Tan Yibing. (2025). Psychometric Evaluation of the Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Scale for Disaster Rescue Nurses in Mainland China. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/9957270
title: CCDNS-DRN: a 33-item, eight-domain, 5-point Likert scale assessing core competencies in disaster nursing of disaster rescue nurses
description: The CCDNS-DRN is a Chinese-language self-report instrument translating the ICN CCDN V2.0 Level II nurse competency requirements for disaster rescue nurses, developed through Beaton's cross-cultural translation process followed by CTT and IRT psychometric evaluation. It "consists of 33 items with eight domains: preparedness and planning (5 items), communication (4 items), incident management (4 items), safety and security (5 items), assessment (4 items), intervention (6 items), recovery (2 items), and law and ethics (3 items)". Each item is scored on a 5-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree, with higher scores implying higher competence. Development included cognitive interviews with DRNs across three rounds, which the authors say identified 28 potential issues.
requirements: Requires respondents who meet DRN inclusion criteria: national nurse qualification, systematic disaster care education, and provincial-level or above disaster nursing specialist certification or EMT membership
constraints: The sample mainly originated from southern China, which the authors state may reduce representativeness and limit generalizability
The scale measures comprehensive disaster nursing competence rather than competence in a specific disaster type
target_learners: Disaster rescue nurses in China (EMT nurses and disaster nursing specialist nurses)
target_learning_goals: Core competencies in disaster nursing across preparation and planning, communication, incident management, safety and security, assessment, intervention, recovery, and law and ethics
examples: Administered online via the WJX app to 401 nurses in Guangdong, Sichuan, Chongqing and other provinces from November 2023 to December 2024
key_sources: Lai Jinjia, Chen Hongyi, Huang Yongqi, Ma Chaoqun, Zeng Ping, Chen Hanxi, Tan Yibing. (2025). Psychometric Evaluation of the Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing Scale for Disaster Rescue Nurses in Mainland China. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/9957270

article_title: Perceived clinical competence and its related factors among registered nurses employed at selected outpatient clinics in Egypt.
citation: Mohamed Rasha A., Alharbi Mohammed Fayez J., Aloufi Rahmah, Abraham Nisha, Taref Nagwa Nabeh, Bauomy Eman Samy, Alkalash Safa H., Marzouk Marzouk M., Almowafy Abeer A. (2024). Perceived clinical competence and its related factors among registered nurses employed at selected outpatient clinics in Egypt. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0314206
title: Clinical Competence Questionnaire (CCQ), Arabic version, for self-assessing nurses' clinical competence
description: The CCQ is a 46-item self-assessment instrument measuring perceived nurses' clinical competence across four domains: professional behaviors (16 competencies), general performance (12), core nursing skills (12), and advanced nursing skills (6), scored on a five-point Likert scale from incapacity to perform to theoretical concept fluency and practical performance under supervision, with total scores from 46 to 230. The study used a translated Arabic version whose "test-retest reliability of the Arabic version in this study was 0.910". Scores were categorized using modified Bloom's cutoff points (competent enough at 80–100%).
requirements: Respondents need sufficient command of the language of administration; the authors translated to Arabic to compensate for nurses' limited English proficiency
At least a baccalaureate degree in nursing sciences and a minimum of 12 months of clinical employment were the study's inclusion criteria
constraints: Measures self-perceived competence, not objectively assessed performance; the authors note self-reported responses may lead to over-reporting or information bias
target_learners: Registered nurses in outpatient and hospital clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of clinical competence and identification of knowledge and skill gaps for continuing professional development
examples: Administered to 450 nurses in Mansoura City, Egypt between January and June 2023, taking 15 to 20 minutes to complete, with a 100% response rate
key_sources: Mohamed Rasha A., Alharbi Mohammed Fayez J., Aloufi Rahmah, Abraham Nisha, Taref Nagwa Nabeh, Bauomy Eman Samy, Alkalash Safa H., Marzouk Marzouk M., Almowafy Abeer A. (2024). Perceived clinical competence and its related factors among registered nurses employed at selected outpatient clinics in Egypt. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0314206

article_title: Students' core competence performance during fundamental nursing practicum: A cross-sectional survey with importance-performance analysis.
citation: Chang, Y.‐H., Shun, S.‐C., & Lin, P.‐C. (2024). Students' core competence performance during fundamental nursing practicum: A cross‐sectional survey with importance–performance analysis. Nursing Open, 11, e70012. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70012
title: Core Competence in Fundamental Nursing Practicum Scale (CCFNPS) with added importance dimension
description: The CCFNPS is a 25-item questionnaire assessing perceived core competence during fundamental nursing practicum, comprising five domains: communication, application of nursing process, basic biomedical science, nursing skills and ability to perform a care process, and professional attitude. In this study an additional importance dimension was added, and "the gaps between students' perceived importance of competence and the perceived performance could be evaluated by subtracting the importance score from the satisfaction score". Cronbach's alpha values were 0.97 and 0.95 for the two dimensions.
requirements: Students must have passed their fundamental nursing practicum within 1 month to respond meaningfully to the scale
constraints: The study evaluated only students' self-perception of core competence performance; the authors note future studies should include the instructors' evaluation
target_learners: junior college nursing students in Taiwan undertaking their fundamental nursing practicum
target_learning_goals: core competencies of fundamental nursing practicum: communication, application of nursing process, basic biomedical science, nursing skills, professional attitude
examples: Used with 659 students across four level-of-care practicum sites to compute importance–performance gaps
key_sources: Chang, Y.‐H., Shun, S.‐C., & Lin, P.‐C. (2024). Students' core competence performance during fundamental nursing practicum: A cross‐sectional survey with importance–performance analysis. Nursing Open, 11, e70012. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70012
